pr_body:
This PR implements the per node readiness check as unix domain socket available if configured in the config file.

## General approach
Open another port in Elasticsearch listening on 9400, but fixed to localhost only. 

The current implementation is using regular sockets because we found Unix Domain Sockets max path too restrictive. Namely Unix Domain Socket path can only be 108 characters long on Linux and 104 on BSD/MacOS. This is limited based on the field sun_path of the sockaddr C struct. Having such a short path to work with would make configuring Elasticsearch too limited and it did cause issues with our tests. The only workaround is to use a relative path, but that would require effectively changing the current working directory, which in Java involves calling native code.

Unix domain sockets based implementation can be found in this commit https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/84375/commits/7452ed2113d80bb34ad43f027818a402abf8c6d0

The socket listen/accept implementation is simplistic but should be sufficient for these purposes, as we don't expect the readiness probe to be called by more than one client at a time. Implementing this using non-blocking sockets will be more complex, as we'll need to implement the listener with both Netty and NIO. 

## Client and protocol
The current implementation is to be used by the k8s TCP probe. The readiness port and listener become open when Elasticsearch is ready, while they are shutdown/closed when it's not. The server doesn't send anything back on the TCP port, it simply disconnects after accepting the connection request by the client.

For the purpose of choosing a port we know is unassigned in IANA, and it doesn't have any existing negative false-positives for security scanners, we took the last port of the Transport port range 9399 to be given as an example in the elasticsearch.yml config file. Respectively, the default ports range for the transport protocol is reduced by 1.

## Performance
Using this TCP probe approach, verifying if Elasticsearch is live takes 10ms with a simple tool like netcat:

```
% time nc localhost 9400
nc localhost 9400  0.00s user 0.01s system 61% cpu 0.011 total
```

Closes #81168
pr_title: Introduce an unauthenticated endpoint for readiness checks

review_comment: Completely closing the socket risks letting someone else grab it while we're unready. Again, maybe no big deal at the moment since we only become unready when shutting down, but maybe not forever. Would it work instead to keep the socket open but only to `accept()` connections on it while we're ready?

I considered that, but I was concerned that it wouldn't work well in all cases. Namely, the probe will connect, but since there's no listener to accept the connection, it will just hang and rely on the probe side connect timeout to expire and disconnect.

I suppose there's no major problem here, it will just take much longer to determine that Elasticsearch is down, relying on a client side timeout instead of an immediately rejected connection. 

If this is acceptable, it's better to just end the thread listener loop and keep the port open.
I'm not 100% sure about this, would be good to get some other opinions. Timing out is not as nice as an outright rejection indeed. Maybe we don't care enough about someone else pinching our port.

I chatted with @ChrisHegarty this morning and we experimented a bit with various options to not run the accept loop. It causes an issue with socket buffers filling up and eventually the ServerSocketChannel gets blocked, causing any connect to timeout until accept runs and clears up the buffers. I think for now I'll stick to the accept thread approach and shutting everything down to avoid problematic scenarios.
I assume these are package private for tests? A comment noting that would be good for future editors to this file
